newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin says to seek audit of French accounts.
newsitem.headline: Jospin says to seek audit of French accounts.

text.p: French opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin has said his party's first act if it wins a snap parliamentary election will be to audit public finances to see if they are as robust as the centre-right coalition says.

"We must establish the reality," the Journal du Dimanche weekly quoted him as saying in an interview. "The first measure we will decide is an audit of the financial situation and of the economic and social accounts of the country."

Jospin, campaigning for the snap May 25-June 1 parliamentary poll, noted Prime Minister Alain Juppe had in 1995 projected a deficit for France's social security system of 17 billion francs in 1996 with a return to balance in 1997.
"Finally in 1996: a deficit of 54 billion and for 1997 there are fears of it again reaching 50 billion," he said.

Jospin reiterated suspicions that Juppe was understating France's financial problems, hoping to win re-election to clear the decks for a harsh brand of capitalism to enable the country to qualify for a single European currency from 1999.

The government says that France is on track with current policies to meet a budget deficit ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product for 1997 set in the Maastricht Treaty on European union as a criterion for joining the euro.
Jospin reiterated that the Socialists also favour the euro, but not at any price.
"If, in order to meet the Maastricht criteria, a new extra austerity cure is necessary, the country simply will not be able to accept it economically and socially. We won't do it," he said.
